author: Vitor
aiExplanation: This function finds the **minimum number of deletions** needed to remove both the smallest and largest elements from an array, where you can only delete from the **front** or the **back**. It first loops through the array once to record the positions of the minimum (`minPos`) and maximum (`maxPos`) values. Then it computes the cost of four possible strategies: delete only from the front until both are gone (`sameSideStart`, which needs `Math.max(minPos, maxPos) + 1` deletions), delete only from the back (`sameSideEnd`, which needs `n - Math.min(minPos, maxPos)` deletions), or remove one element from each end (`oppositeStart` and `oppositeEnd`, which take the min from the front and the max from the back, or vice versa). Finally, `Math.min` picks the cheapest of the four options, giving an efficient **O(n)** solution with a single pass and constant extra work.

notes: Simplified for better performance, not enough test coverage to allow for proper performance testing.
aiExplanation: This function computes the **minimum number of deletions** required to remove both the smallest and largest values from an array when deletions are only allowed from the **front** or the **back**. A single loop finds where the minimum and maximum live (`minPos` and `maxPos`), and these are then simplified into `earliest` (the one closer to the start) and `latest` (the one closer to the end). Only three strategies matter: delete everything from the front up to and including `latest` (`latest + 1` deletions), delete everything from the back down to and including `earliest` (`n - earliest` deletions), or split the work by taking `earliest` out through the front and `latest` out through the back (`earliest + 1 + n - latest` deletions). The answer is the smallest of the three via `Math.min`, and because the positions are ordered up front, this version avoids checking a redundant fourth case while staying **O(n)** with one pass over the array.
